title: Lesson 1. What is Gaussian Splatting, and what problem does it solve?

cells.source:
We have a few photographs of a mug from different sides. The idea is to rotate it on a screen and look from a place where the camera **never stood**. The photographs are there. What would turn them into that kind of viewer?

We will start by rotating a small scene, taking it apart, changing a few numbers, and watching what happens to the image. Then we will follow the path from photographs to a finished model: what it stores, how training finds those values, and what the program does when we simply move the camera.

Along the way, we will look at a limitation that is easy to miss: being able to look behind an object does not mean we have discovered what its back really looks like.

No matrices or derivatives are needed yet. First, let us see what we are working with. In lesson 2, we will take one soft spot and work through its mathematics one operation at a time.

## 1. A Small Scene

We will start with a colored sphere above a plane. It is a small scene: **192 Gaussians**, with 128 on the sphere and 64 on the plane. Their positions, shapes, and colors are already specified in the code. Nothing has been trained from photographs here; this example lets us explore how the pieces work.

The camera is simplified too: distant objects do not shrink with perspective as they would in an ordinary photograph. This is an **orthographic** camera, with parallel projection directions. It makes the shapes easier to examine at first. We will introduce perspective and full rendering later.

To decide which footprint goes over another, the viewer compares the depths of their centers. That ordering can be wrong when shapes intersect in complicated ways. It is enough for our first experiments; we will return to overlap later.
display(scene_overview(language=LANG))

These are three views of **the same data from the same viewpoint**. Each mode adds something:

| Mode | What is shown | What to look for |
|---|---|---|
| **Centers** | The position of each Gaussian | Gaps remain between the points. The size and softness of each footprint are still hidden. |
| **Contours** | A line at the same influence level around each Gaussian | Size and orientation are now visible. Influence continues beyond the contour, growing weaker. |
| **Composite image** | Soft colored footprints that overlap | The contributions combine into a more continuous image. |

Here, each contour is drawn where the footprint's weight is about **61% of its weight at the center**. We use the same level for every Gaussian so we can compare their shapes. In the next lesson, we will unpack what this weight means and how to calculate it.

Switching modes has not removed any centers. We are displaying the same collection of numbers in different ways.
display(scene_lab(language=LANG))

## 2. What Changes as the Camera and Parameters Move

Five changes are easy to follow in the image.

1. **Three modes with a fixed camera.** The plane has gaps between its centers. In Composite image mode, contributions around the existing centers fill those gaps.
2. **Camera orbit and view elevation.** The first slider takes the camera around the scene; the second changes the view from above to a view from the side. The plane looks broad from one direction and almost like a strip from another. The scene itself has stayed the same.
3. **One Gaussian in isolation.** The “Only the selected Gaussian” switch leaves one element on screen. Its number is called its index: its place in a list. That number does not inherently tell the program “chair,” “wall,” or “sphere.” Its contour shows the shape; Composite image mode shows its soft color contribution.
4. **Opacity 0, about 0.5, and 1.** In Composite image mode, zero makes the color contribution disappear. A larger value makes it stronger. In Centers mode, the point is still there because the element remains in the data.
5. **The whole scene and Reset.** Among all the other Gaussians, a change to one element can be easy to miss. Reset brings back the original parameters and viewpoint, giving the experiment the same starting image again.

We have already produced several different images without training anything. Each camera movement asked the program to compute another view of the same collection of elements.

## 3. Where does a new view come from?

Back to the mug. In the front photograph, the handle is on the right. From the other side of the table, it may appear on the left or disappear behind the body. Stretching the first photograph cannot give us those changes: it only records pixel colors from one viewpoint.

A photograph is a flat grid of colored pixels. Each pixel gives a color at one location **in that photograph**. That value alone does not tell us what a camera would see after moving one step to the left.

We therefore need a **scene representation**: data from which we can build images for different cameras. Building an image is called **rendering**. When we choose a camera position absent from the input photographs, we are doing **novel-view synthesis**.

In Gaussian Splatting, those data are a collection of Gaussians. The renderer takes their parameters and assembles an image for the chosen camera. Reconstruction fits the parameters to the photographs so that views from the input cameras increasingly resemble the original images.

Matching the photographs is already useful. How accurately the model describes the whole scene, including hidden surfaces, is something we still need to check. We will return to that when we discuss unseen sides.

## 4. What does one Gaussian store?

A soft spot of paint gives us a useful first picture: it can move, stretch, rotate, or become more noticeable. In 3D, we have a distribution of influence in space; projecting it produces a footprint on the screen. Paint is a useful analogy for the softness. It does not imply liquid behavior or a hard shell.

Each selected element has a card with its parameters. The Sphere and Plane labels were assigned manually when the example was built. No object recognition was needed to produce those labels.

Now let us examine four groups of properties. We will use simple numbers below, so they may differ from the selected element's values in the card.

### Position: where we put the center

On a plane, a position needs two coordinates; in space, it needs three. For example, **(0, 0, 1)**. In our experiment's coordinates, that means zero displacement along both directions of the plane and a height of 1 above it. Here, the vertical direction is called **z**; other programs may arrange their axes differently. The unit is arbitrary, so 1 does not necessarily mean one meter.

The Gaussian's weight is greatest at its center. Moving the center moves the entire distribution with it.

### Shape: which way to stretch it

An ordinary balloon and a flattened one make a useful comparison. The second can spread influence widely along a surface and narrowly across it. Rotation sets the directions in which it stretches.

For example, scales **(0.2, 0.2, 0.2)** are equal along the Gaussian's three local directions. Increasing the first to **0.4** makes the distribution wider in that direction. There is still no hard outer edge: influence gradually fades as we move away from the center.

In lesson 2, we will first explore one such scale on a line. Then we will add a second direction, build a footprint on a plane, and return to 3D.

### Color: what color the footprint adds

Our example stores color as three **RGB** components: red, green, and blue. Each ranges from 0 to 1. Then **(1, 0, 0)** gives red, **(0, 1, 0)** gives green, and **(1, 1, 1)** gives white.

Each Gaussian in this scene has a constant color. In full 3DGS, color can depend on viewing direction. That helps describe, for example, a shiny object's visible color changing as we walk around it. We will reach that color representation in lesson 15.

### Opacity: how noticeable its contribution is

The opacity slider ranges from **0 to 1**. At 0, the Gaussian adds nothing to the image's color. A larger value makes its contribution stronger.

Even with opacity **1**, the footprint stays soft. Influence is stronger at the center and weaker farther away; the entire footprint does not become an opaque plate. Neighboring elements and their overlap order also affect the final color.

That is why the control is called **opacity**: a larger number means a stronger contribution. Calling it transparency would suggest the opposite direction.

## 5. Why build a scene from many footprints?

One soft footprint only gets us so far. Several well-placed Gaussians can describe a color transition, an edge, or a surface region. Our sphere is built from many such elements, although no individual element inherently knows it is “part of a sphere.”

In isolation, one Gaussian describes very little. Once the rest of the scene returns, that same element becomes part of a surface.

It is tempting to jump from this to “add more Gaussians, get a better image.” So far, though, we have only added parameters to adjust. An accurate image needs suitable positions, shapes, and other values, enough observations, and a training process that can fit them.

A million randomly scattered Gaussians will not assemble themselves into an accurate room. There is no universal element count that makes every scene photorealistic.

The viewer lets us see the elements working together. The next course block will explore how to find their positions and shapes from images.

## 6. From photographs to a finished model

Our scene had a convenient starting point: all the parameters were already in the code. For a real object, we still need to find them. Let us follow where they come from when we start with photographs.
display(pipeline_figure(language=LANG))

| Stage | What we start with | What we get |
|---|---|---|
| **Capture** | A static scene and a camera | Photographs from different positions with shared regions of the scene |
| **Camera and point reconstruction** | Photographs with common visible details | Estimated camera parameters and a sparse point cloud; COLMAP often does this work |
| **Gaussian initialization** | Initial points and associated information | A first collection of Gaussians to begin training |
| **Training** | Gaussians, cameras, and input photographs | Adjusted parameters whose rendered images match the photographs more closely |
| **Viewing** | A saved model and a chosen camera | An image from the requested viewpoint |

Camera positions also have to be estimated. Errors at that stage make it harder for training to bring the model into agreement with the photographs.

### What training does

We place a virtual camera at the position of one input photograph and render the current model. Now we can place the two images side by side: where does the color already match, where is the object slightly displaced, and where has a detail disappeared?

We turn those differences into a numerical error. The algorithm changes parameters to reduce it, then takes another viewpoint and repeats the comparison. Basic 3DGS also adds and removes Gaussians. Adjusting existing elements and changing the number of elements are two related parts of the process.

The sequence is: **render an image → compare it with the photograph → adjust the parameters → repeat**. In lessons 6–9, we will calculate an error ourselves and work through an update with actual numbers. Full 3D training and changes to the Gaussian count come in lessons 16–17.

### What happens when we just view the model

During viewing, the parameters have already been found and saved. After the camera moves, the renderer uses those parameters to compute the next frame. It does not have to return to the photographs and train the model again after every turn. Training time and viewing speed are therefore separate measurements.

The [original 3DGS project page](https://repo-sam.inria.fr/fungraph/3d-gaussian-splatting/) has real reconstructions and comparisons with reference images. Our sphere and plane are still a manually built example for exploring the parameters; those reconstructions show the result of training from photographs.

In Visual Comparisons on the project page, Ours and Ground Truth show the method's result and a reference for the same viewpoint. Edges, fine textures, and highlights reveal which details match and which differ. Ground Truth is the reference for comparison; the label alone does not tell us that this particular frame was used for training. This is an extra experiment. The main lesson exercises work locally.

## 7. What about the side nobody photographed?

Let us return to the limitation from the beginning. The next diagram shows an object and the surrounding cameras from above, making each camera's visible area easier to follow. It does not simulate training or reconstruction quality.
display(coverage_figure(language=LANG))

There are three cases in the diagram:

1. **The region is visible to camera A.** Its photograph already contains an observation of that region.
2. **The region is hidden from A but visible to camera B.** The second photograph adds something the first one is missing.
3. **The region is hidden from both cameras.** These observations do not directly tell us what it looks like.

Suppose we have two boxes with identical fronts. One has a red back; the other has a blue back. The camera records only the fronts, without capturing either back directly or through reflections. The photographs will be identical. They cannot tell us which color was behind either box.

The program can still draw a back wall. To check its color, though, we need an observation from behind. If we assume a color instead, that assumption brings in information from elsewhere; it did not come from the input photographs.

New viewpoints are not all hopeless. We can move the camera to a new position and see a surface already well covered by other photographs. Difficulties arise where observations are scarce or inconsistent.

Our example defines the whole sphere, so the program knows its back too. We can freely orbit it, but that has not tested the recovery of surfaces absent from every photograph.

## 8. Other ways to store a scene

We can now compare Gaussian Splatting with other approaches using the same question each time: **what is stored, and how does it become an image?**

| Representation | What it stores | What to remember |
|---|---|---|
| **Polygon mesh** | Vertices and faces, usually with materials or textures | The surface is explicit, making it useful for editing and interaction. An artist or an image-reconstruction algorithm can build it. |
| **Voxels** | Values in cells of a three-dimensional grid | Space is divided into cells, like a volumetric version of pixels. A dense grid grows quickly with resolution; sparse versions store only the needed parts. |
| **Point cloud** | Point coordinates, sometimes with color and other attributes | Useful for storing measurements and initial geometry. The viewer decides how to display the points. |
| **NeRF and related methods** | In the original NeRF, density depends on position; color also depends on viewing direction | A neural network computes these values in the original NeRF. Other methods change both the representation and computation, so their speeds differ. |
| **Gaussian Splatting** | A collection of Gaussians with adjustable parameters | Individual elements are projected and blended. Each can be inspected, but its relationship to an entire object still needs to be established. |

Each approach has different variants. For example, [Instant-NGP](https://nvlabs.github.io/instant-ngp/) is a useful reason not to label the entire NeRF family “always slow.”

The original 3DGS experiments combined high-quality images with fast rendering. For any new scene, quality and speed still need to be measured: the data, implementation, image resolution, work per frame, and computer all affect the result.

Gaussians are also convenient for learning. We can pick an element, change a number, and see what happened to the image. That is how we will approach the next lessons.

## 9. A Few Questions About the Scene

Here are five situations from the same experiment, each with an explanation that can be checked in the scene.

### Exercise 1. What did the switch change?

The camera stays still. Switching from Centers to Composite image leaves fewer visible gaps. Where did the more continuous image come from? Were new points added to the data?

<details>
<summary>Worked answer</summary>

The list still contains 192 elements. Centers mode only showed their positions. The renderer now also uses shape, color, and opacity: each contribution spreads around its center, and neighboring footprints overlap. No new elements were needed to change the image.

</details>

### Exercise 2. Why is the point still there?

One Gaussian is shown in isolation with opacity 0. Its color contribution disappears in Composite image mode. Why is its point still there in Centers mode?

<details>
<summary>Worked answer</summary>

We set the contribution to zero without deleting the element from the list. Its coordinates are unchanged. Centers mode shows those data, so it can draw a point even for a Gaussian that currently adds nothing to the image's color. Removing the element from the list would require a separate deletion operation.

</details>

### Exercise 3. Are front photographs enough?

A box was photographed only from the front. The resulting model has a blue back. Can we say that its color was recovered correctly?

<details>
<summary>Worked answer</summary>

Not from these photographs, if the back was never observed and no additional information about it is available. Red and blue backs could have produced identical photographs from the front. We need a rear observation or an explicitly stated assumption about the color. One rendered blue wall is not enough to check the result.

</details>

### Exercise 4. What is needed for the next frame?

We have trained and saved the model. Now we rotate the camera a little. Do we need to fit all the Gaussians to the input photographs again?

<details>
<summary>Worked answer</summary>

For ordinary viewing, the saved parameters and the new camera position are enough for the renderer to build the next frame. Training does not need to start again. But if the model describes that view poorly, rotating the camera alone will not fix its parameters.

</details>

### Exercise 5. Would another thousand Gaussians help?

Suppose a thousand random Gaussians are added to a model. Does it necessarily reproduce the input photographs more accurately now?

<details>
<summary>Worked answer</summary>

So far, we have only gained more parameters. Those still need suitable values. Random positions and colors can spoil the image while giving the renderer more work. A comparison with observations reveals whether anything improved. That includes viewpoints held out for evaluation rather than used in training.

</details>

## 10. What we can now explain

We started with a colored sphere and found a collection of numbers behind it. The model stores Gaussian positions, shapes, colors, and opacities. The renderer takes those data and a chosen camera and produces an image.

The same collection can be shown as centers, contours, or soft footprints. Contours help us inspect the shapes without cutting off influence at their boundaries. Reconstruction fits parameters to observations; viewing uses the values already found.

The observations still set a limit: an extra photograph can reveal a hidden region. If a surface appears in none of our observations, we may simply have no reliable answer about its appearance.

Now we can unpack the soft footprint itself. How do we put numbers to influence that is strongest at the center and gradually fades away? In [lesson 2](#/en/2), we will start on a line, build a bell curve one operation at a time, and calculate its value at a selected point by hand.

## Sources and additional examples

- [Kerbl et al. — 3D Gaussian Splatting for Real-Time Radiance Field Rendering](https://repo-sam.inria.fr/fungraph/3d-gaussian-splatting/): the original work, video, and result comparisons.
- [COLMAP — Tutorial](https://colmap.github.io/tutorial.html): reconstructing cameras and structure from images, with capture recommendations.
- [Mildenhall et al. — NeRF](https://www.matthewtancik.com/nerf): the original neural radiance field representation.
- [Müller et al. — Instant-NGP](https://nvlabs.github.io/instant-ngp/): an example of how changes to representation and implementation accelerate neural graphics methods.

title: Lesson 2 — One Gaussian on a Line: Taking Apart the Bell Curve

cells.source:
We start with one bell curve to see how it works. First, we'll move it around and change its width. Then we'll pick a point and work out, by hand, why it sits at that particular height. Along the way, we'll unpack every operation in the formula.

Ordinary arithmetic is enough to get started. Derivatives, matrices, and probability theory can wait. For now, we're working with a **one-dimensional** Gaussian: it takes one coordinate and returns one number.

In lesson 1, we built an image from soft spots. Now we'll draw a line through one spot and see how its influence changes along that line: stronger in the middle, weaker farther away. We'll describe that influence with a number called a weight. Pixel colors and overlapping spots will come in later lessons.

## 1. The Bell Curve and Three Parameters

The graph has a center, a width, and a point where we measure the weight. First comes their effect on the image. Then we calculate the Gaussian step by step, using ordinary arithmetic.

display(gaussian_figure(mu=2, sigma=2, x=4, language=LANG))
display(gaussian_lab(language=LANG))

The formula can wait for a moment. Three changes are visible in the plot:

1. The center moves from 2 to −2. The bell moves, but its shape and peak height stay the same.
2. The center returns to 2, and the width decreases from 2 to 1. The bell becomes narrower, while its peak remains at 1.
3. The width returns to 2, and the measurement point moves along the graph. Each location has its own weight; the bell itself stays the same.

The fixed axes show the moving bell against the same scale. For the calculations below, we use **center 2 and width 2**, starting at point **4**.

## 2. How to Read One Point on the Graph

We can use an ordinary ruler. We selected the mark at 4 and want to know the weight there.

| Notation | Read it as | What it means here |
|---|---|---|
| $x$ | “x” | The coordinate we inspect: 4 |
| $\mu$ | “mu” | The center of the bell: 2 |
| $\sigma$ | “sigma” | The width scale: 2; it must be greater than zero |
| $f(x)$ | “f of x” | The weight we'll get at point $x$ |

The parentheses in $f(x)$ identify the function's input. This is **not** multiplication of a letter $f$ by a number $x$. Here, “function” simply means a rule: receive a coordinate, perform some operations, return a number.

For our bell, $f(2)=1$: the center has the maximum weight. Writing $f(4)$ means “calculate the weight at 4.” We will obtain approximately 0.606531.

Changing $\mu$ or $\sigma$ changes the bell itself. Changing $x$ just picks where on that bell we check the weight.

## 3. First Step: Measuring from the Center

A coordinate alone does not tell us whether we are far from the bell. The point 100 can be exactly at its center if the center is also 100.

We therefore subtract the center first:

$$
d=x-\mu.
$$

We'll call this **displacement from the center** $d$, so we don't have to write out the subtraction every time. With $x=4$ and $\mu=2$:

$$
d=4-2=2.
$$

We are two units to the right of the center. Now we take $x=0$:

$$
d=0-2=-2.
$$

We are two units to the left. The sign records the side, while the magnitude 2 records how far away we are. At the center itself, $d=2-2=0$.

We want points equally far to the left and right to have the same weight. So far, we've got different numbers: $2$ and $-2$. In two steps, squaring will make them match.

## 4. Second Step: Measuring Displacement in Units of Width

We're two units from the center. That could be far away for a narrow spot or quite close for a wide one. Distance alone isn't enough: we also need to compare it with the spot's width.

$$
u=\frac{d}{\sigma}.
$$

The fraction bar means division. We'll call the result $u$: we're now measuring **displacement in units of width**. With our numbers:

$$
u=\frac{2}{2}=1.
$$

The point is one width to the right of the center. On the left, we obtain $(-2)/2=-1$.

If the point and center stay fixed but we set $\sigma=1$, then $u=2/1=2$: the same point is now two widths from the center. If we set $\sigma=4$, then $u=2/4=0.5$: only half a width away.

We express $x,\mu,\sigma$ in the same units. If the coordinates are in centimeters, the width must be in centimeters too. In “2 cm / 2 cm,” the centimeters cancel, leaving just 1. We call this number **dimensionless**. We've found how many widths separate the point from the center; choosing centimeters or meters doesn't change that answer.

$\sigma$ sets the width scale. It doesn't measure the spot's full width or mark a boundary: our bell has no sharp edge at all.

## 5. Third Step: Making the Left and Right Sides Match

We square the relative displacement:

$$
q=u^2=u\cdot u.
$$

The small raised 2 means “multiply the number by itself.” The centered dot means multiplication.

To the right of the center:

$$
q=1^2=1\cdot1=1.
$$

To the left:

$$
q=(-1)^2=(-1)\cdot(-1)=1.
$$

The product of two negative numbers is positive, so both sides produce the same result. At the center, $q=0^2=0$. Two widths away, $q=2^2=4$; three widths away, $q=3^2=9$.

After squaring, the left and right sides match, and the numbers grow faster as we move away from the center. So far, though, we've got the opposite of what we need: zero at the center, more farther away. Our **weight** should be greatest at the center and get smaller as we move out.

We're using a square because we're building a Gaussian. We could use absolute value — magnitude without a sign — and still get a symmetric spot, but its profile would be different. There are plenty of soft shapes; we're working out how to build this particular one.

## 6. Fourth Step: Dividing by Two and Adding a Minus Sign

Now we divide the square by 2 and change its sign:

$$
t=-\frac{q}{2}.
$$

We'll call this step's result $t$. The letter has nothing to do with time here; it's just another short name. Division comes first, followed by the minus sign:

- at the center: $q=0$, so $t=-0/2=0$;
- one width away: $q=1$, so $t=-1/2=-0.5$;
- two widths away: $q=4$, so $t=-4/2=-2$;
- three widths away: $q=9$, so $t=-9/2=-4.5$.

As we move farther from the center, the number becomes more negative. The next operation turns that into a smaller **positive** weight.

The divisor 2 affects how quickly the weight will decrease. It's part of the usual Gaussian formula and sets the relationship between the bell's width and its scale parameter. Removing the two while keeping the same $\sigma$ makes the bell narrower. Below, we'll compare the plots and calculate the difference. A bell curve still works without that particular divisor.

## 7. The Final Step: What exp and the Number e Mean

We have reached $t=-0.5$, but this is not a weight yet. We need an operation where:

- input 0 gives output 1;
- a negative input gives a positive number below 1;
- a more negative input gives a smaller output.

The exponential does this:

$$
\exp(t)=e^t.
$$

On the left, “exp” is a function's name and $t$ in parentheses is its input. The right side expresses the same operation as a power. $e$ is a constant, approximately **2.71828**; $t$ is the exponent. “Approximately” means that only the first few digits are shown.

An exponent of −0.5 may not look very helpful yet. We can start with the familiar number 2 and work our way to that notation.

### Positive, Zero, and Negative Exponents

Positive integer powers are straightforward:

$$
2^1=2,\qquad 2^2=2\cdot2=4,\qquad 2^3=2\cdot2\cdot2=8.
$$

Going from exponent 3 to exponent 2 divides by 2: $8/2=4$. One more step down gives $4/2=2$. Continuing the same rule gives:

| Exponent | Operation | Value |
|---|---|---:|
| 1 | Starting number | 2 |
| 0 | $2/2$ | 1 |
| −1 | $1/2$ | 0.5 |
| −2 | $0.5/2$ | 0.25 |

Thus $2^0=1$, while $2^{-2}=1/(2\cdot2)=1/4$.

The same rule works for any positive base, including $e$:

$$
e^0=1,\qquad e^{-1}=\frac{1}{e},\qquad e^{-2}=\frac{1}{e^2}.
$$

**A minus sign in the exponent does not make the answer negative.** It tells us to take one and divide it by the result of the positive power. This is called taking the reciprocal.

### A Half Power

What does an exponent of 0.5 mean? It is half of one: $0.5=1/2$. For a positive number, exponent $1/2$ means the **square root**.

A square root is a nonnegative number that gives the original number when multiplied by itself. For example, $\sqrt{9}=3$, because $3\cdot3=9$. The symbol **√** is read as “square root.”

Two equal halves of an exponent add up to exponent 1. Thus $e^{1/2}\cdot e^{1/2}=e^1=e$, which means $e^{1/2}=\sqrt{e}$. Applying the negative-exponent rule gives:

$$
e^{-0.5}=\frac{1}{e^{0.5}}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{e}}.
$$

The approximate calculation is:

$$
e\approx2.71828,\qquad
\sqrt{e}\approx1.64872,\qquad
\frac{1}{1.64872}\approx0.60653.
$$

The symbol $\approx$ means “approximately equals.” Python uses a more accurate value of $e$ in the actual calculation, so we round only for display.

Other fractional exponents extend the same idea. For example, exponent $1/4$ gives the number that must be multiplied by itself four times to recover the base. For an arbitrary real exponent, the exponential continues these values into a continuous curve. In the code, `math.exp` calculates these powers without a separate hand calculation for each one.

### Where the Particular Number e Comes From

So far, we've treated $e$ as a number we were simply given. We can approximate it using a few multiplications.

We start at 1. Increasing it by 100% once gives $1\cdot(1+1)=2$. Now we split the increase into two successive steps of 50% **of the current value**:

$$
1\cdot(1+1/2)\cdot(1+1/2)=1\cdot1.5\cdot1.5=2.25.
$$

The result exceeds 2 because the second step increases 1.5, not the original one.

If we split the process into $n$ equal steps, each step multiplies the current result by $1+1/n$. The letter $n$ is the number of steps, a positive integer. After $n$ multiplications, we obtain:

$$
a_n=\left(1+\frac{1}{n}\right)^n.
$$

We've named the result $a_n$. The small subscript reminds us which $n$ we chose. Reading the expression from the inside, we divide 1 by $n$, add 1, then multiply that result by itself $n$ times.

As $n$ increases, the results get closer and closer to one number: $e$. We call it the limit of this sequence — the value it approaches as the step count increases without end. With any finite $n$, we have only an approximation.

A short Python example checks this numerically. In Python, `**` means exponentiation. The `.8f` asks for eight digits after the decimal point when printing; it doesn't change the calculation.

import math

for n in [1, 2, 10, 100, 1000, 10000]:
    approximation = (1 + 1 / n) ** n
    print(f"n = {n:5d} -> {approximation:.8f}")

print(f"math.e     -> {math.e:.8f}")

We now know where the number $e$ comes from, and so far arithmetic has been enough. An exponential with this base is part of the usual Gaussian formula. But a soft-looking spot alone cannot tell us to use $e$, a square, or the factor $1/2$. We've chosen a specific model for our spot, and we're working through how it behaves.

Here are the values needed for the calculation. In `math.exp(t)`, the `math` module contains mathematical functions and `exp` calculates $e^t$. The loop assigns each of the four listed values to `t` in turn.

The exponent $-4.5$ is far below zero, but $\exp(-4.5)$ is still **positive** — approximately 0.011109. This is 1.1109% of the peak because $0.011109\cdot100=1.1109$.

Percent means “parts per hundred.” Here, we've taken the peak weight of 1 as 100% and are comparing the other weights with it. This doesn't measure a probability of reaching a point or a fraction of the area under the curve.

## 8. Combining the Operations in One Formula

Our recipe is:

$$
d=x-\mu,\qquad
u=\frac{d}{\sigma},\qquad
q=u^2,\qquad
t=-\frac{q}{2},\qquad
f(x)=\exp(t).
$$

At each step, we use the previous result. Replacing the short names with the operations themselves puts the whole sequence into one expression:

$$
f(x)=\exp\left(-\frac{1}{2}
\left(\frac{x-\mu}{\sigma}\right)^2\right).
$$

Multiplying by $1/2$ is the same as dividing by 2. We can expand the squared fraction:

$$
\begin{aligned}
\left(\frac{x-\mu}{\sigma}\right)^2
&=\frac{x-\mu}{\sigma}\cdot\frac{x-\mu}{\sigma}\\
&=\frac{(x-\mu)(x-\mu)}{\sigma\cdot\sigma}\\
&=\frac{(x-\mu)^2}{\sigma^2}.
\end{aligned}
$$

We multiplied the numerators together and the denominators together. We can now write the formula more compactly:

$$
\boxed{f(x)=\exp\left(-\frac{(x-\mu)^2}{2\sigma^2}\right)}.
$$

Now we can see where the squared width at the bottom came from: we squared the **whole fraction containing the displacement**. The parentheses around $x-\mu$ set the order: we subtract the center first, then square the result.

The plots below show those same operations. The whole line changes at each step, while the marked point passes through the numbers we just calculated.
display(construction_figure(language=LANG))

## 9. Complete Calculation: Point 4, Center 2, Width 2

The calculation for our point fits into one table. Every step is already familiar:

| Step | Calculation | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| Displacement | $4-2=2$ | Two units to the right of the center |
| Divide by width | $2/2=1$ | One width from the center |
| Square | $1\cdot1=1$ | The same result on both sides |
| Divide by 2 and negate | $-1/2=-0.5$ | An exponent for a decreasing weight |
| Exponential | $e^{-0.5}\approx0.606531$ | The weight at the selected point |

Thus **$f(4)\approx0.606531$**. On the graph, it is the point's height above coordinate 4. On the strip, it is the corresponding brightness.

The same calculation follows in Python. Variable names follow the stages: `offset` is the displacement, `relative` the relative displacement, `squared` its square, `exponent` the power's exponent, and `weight` the final weight. In code, `=` stores the result on the right in the variable on the left.

x = 4.0
mu = 2.0
sigma = 2.0

offset = x - mu
relative = offset / sigma
squared = relative * relative
exponent = -squared / 2
weight = math.exp(exponent)

print(f"x - mu                 = {offset:.6f}")
print(f"(x - mu) / sigma       = {relative:.6f}")
print(f"relative * relative    = {squared:.6f}")
print(f"-squared / 2           = {exponent:.6f}")
print(f"exp(exponent)          = {weight:.6f}")
cells.output:
x - mu                 = 2.000000
(x - mu) / sigma       = 1.000000
relative * relative    = 1.000000
-squared / 2           = -0.500000
exp(exponent)          = 0.606531

cells.source:
### The Other Side and the Peak

For $x=0$, $\mu=2$, $\sigma=2$:

$$
d=0-2=-2,\qquad
u=-2/2=-1,\qquad
q=(-1)\cdot(-1)=1,
$$

$$
t=-1/2=-0.5,\qquad
f(0)=e^{-0.5}\approx0.606531.
$$

We got the same weight as on the right. The bell looked symmetric in the plot; now the numbers match too.

For $x=2$, exactly at the center:

$$
d=2-2=0,\qquad
u=0/2=0,\qquad
q=0\cdot0=0,
$$

$$
t=-0/2=0,\qquad
f(2)=e^0=1.
$$

With positive width, the same sequence always holds at the center: zero displacement → zero exponent → weight 1.

For $x=6$: $d=6-2=4$, $u=4/2=2$, $q=2\cdot2=4$, $t=-4/2=-2$, so $f(6)=e^{-2}\approx0.135335$.

For $x=8$: $d=8-2=6$, $u=6/2=3$, $q=3\cdot3=9$, $t=-9/2=-4.5$, so $f(8)=e^{-4.5}\approx0.011109$.

Python can go through those steps for all five points. The loop repeats our calculation and collects the results in a table.

mu = 2.0
sigma = 2.0

print(" x    offset  relative  squared  exponent    weight")
for x in [2.0, 4.0, 0.0, 6.0, 8.0]:
    offset = x - mu
    relative = offset / sigma
    squared = relative * relative
    exponent = -squared / 2
    weight = math.exp(exponent)
    print(
        f"{x:3.0f}  {offset:8.1f}  {relative:8.1f}  "
        f"{squared:7.1f}  {exponent:8.1f}  {weight:10.6f}"
    )

## 10. What Width Changes and Why the Formula Contains a Two

First, we keep $x=4$ and $\mu=2$ while changing the width from 2 to 1:

$$
d=4-2=2,\quad
u=2/1=2,\quad
q=2\cdot2=4,\quad
t=-4/2=-2,
$$

$$
f(4)=e^{-2}\approx0.135335.
$$

The weight went from 0.606531 to 0.135335. We didn't move the point, but narrowing the bell put it farther from the center **in units of width**. Its weight fell, while the weight at the center stayed at 1.

Now we return to $\sigma=2$ and temporarily remove the divisor 2 from the exponent. At $x=4$, the relative displacement is 1:

- with the divisor: exponent $-1/2=-0.5$, weight approximately 0.606531;
- without the divisor: exponent $-1=-1$, weight approximately 0.367879.

Without the divisor, the weight falls off faster. We've effectively narrowed the bell without changing the number in the width setting.

We can obtain the same narrower profile while keeping the usual formula and changing its width. The numbers make this visible. With the old width 2 and the divisor removed, the denominator is $2^2=4$. In the usual formula, we need a new positive scale $w$ such that:

$$
2w^2=4.
$$

Here, $w$ is just a name for the new width. Dividing both sides by 2 gives $w^2=2$. Therefore $w=\sqrt{2}\approx1.414214$. This is less than 2.

The factor $1/2$ is therefore **part of a scale convention**, not the only possible way to draw a bell. In statistics, the scale $\sigma$ under this convention equals the standard deviation of the corresponding normalized Gaussian. For now, we choose $\sigma$ with the slider or in the code; calculating a standard deviation from a dataset can wait.

On the left, we change the width in the same formula. On the right, we keep the width setting and look at what happens when we remove the two.
display(width_figure(language=LANG))

## 11. What Our Weight Actually Tells Us

Our Gaussian always has a peak of 1. It's called **unnormalized**: we haven't added a factor to make the area under its graph equal to one. That choice matters when the width changes.

Coloring in the area under the curve makes the difference visible. Stretching the bell horizontally while keeping its height increases the colored area. That's fine for our weight. If we were building a probability density, we'd need to keep that area equal to one; that isn't our task yet.

Our 0.606531 tells us how strong the influence is at this point relative to the center. We can't read it as “a 60.6531% probability of being at exactly this point.” We haven't calculated the Gaussian's full opacity or the final pixel color either.

Later, we'll add color, an opacity parameter, and blending with neighboring Gaussians. For now, we needed to understand one part: **how influence decreases smoothly as we move away from the center**.

A flashlight's spot helps us picture this. A real flashlight may have a different profile, though: the formula we just unpacked defines the exact shape of our spot.

## 12. Zero Width, Negative Coordinates, and the Tails of the Bell

**The width is greater than zero.** With $\sigma=0$, we would have to divide by zero. The formula is undefined even at the center, where it would require $0/0$. We won't use −2 as a width either. Squaring it would give the same profile as 2, but a negative length isn't useful here. We'll stick to $\sigma>0$.

**Coordinates can be negative.** If $x$ or the center $\mu$ is below zero, we've simply picked a mark to the left of zero on the ruler. The restriction on the sign of the width doesn't apply to coordinates.

**The weight cannot exceed 1.** A square is nonnegative, so after division and negation the exponent is at most zero. For the positive exponential, exponent zero gives 1 and a negative exponent gives less than 1.

**The bell doesn't end at three widths.** At distance $3\sigma$, the weight is $e^{-4.5}\approx0.011109$. At $4\sigma$: relative displacement 4 → square 16 → exponent $-16/2=-8$ → weight $e^{-8}\approx0.000335$.

In exact mathematics, any finite coordinate and positive finite width produce a weight greater than zero. On a computer, an extremely small value can round down to zero because numbers have limited storage precision. That is a computational limit, not a break in the mathematical curve.

Renderers sometimes discard weak tails to produce images faster. But a distance of $3\sigma$ alone cannot tell us that a contribution is safe to ignore. We also need to consider opacity, neighboring elements, and how accurate we want the image to be.

## 13. A Function for Experiments

We can put our operations into a function. It takes `x`, `mu`, and `sigma` and returns the weight. The line with `sigma <= 0` checks the width: if it's zero or negative, the function stops and shows an error.

These experiments use ordinary finite numbers, without infinity or special values such as `NaN`. Each of the five operations has its own line, matching the steps of the calculation.

def gaussian_weight(x, mu, sigma):
    if sigma <= 0:
        raise ValueError("sigma must be greater than zero")

    offset = x - mu
    relative = offset / sigma
    squared = relative * relative
    exponent = -squared / 2
    return math.exp(exponent)


x = 4.0
mu = 2.0
sigma = 2.0

print(f"weight = {gaussian_weight(x, mu, sigma):.6g}")

Each experiment has two results to compare: the expected change in the graph and the number returned by the code.

| One changed value; the others stay at their defaults | Question |
|---|---|
| `x = 0.0` | Does the weight equal the value at 4? Why? |
| `mu = 4.0` | What weight will the selected point at 4 have? |
| `sigma = 1.0` | Will the weight at 4 increase or decrease? |
| `sigma = 4.0` | How far away is the point in units of width now? |
| `sigma = 0.0` | Why should the function stop rather than produce an image? |

Each experiment changes one parameter while keeping the others at their defaults. The plot at the start of the lesson shows these changes directly.

For zero width, we call only `gaussian_weight`. It raises a `ValueError`: the check prevents division by zero. There is no plot for this case. Returning to `sigma=2` restores the normal calculation.

<details>
<summary>Answers to the parameter experiments</summary>

**Point on the left, $x=0$.** Displacement $0-2=-2$, relative displacement $-2/2=-1$, square $(-1)^2=1$, exponent $-1/2=-0.5$. The weight is $e^{-0.5}\approx0.606531$. Squaring gives the same result as for $x=4$.

**Center at the measurement point, $\mu=4$.** Displacement $4-4=0$, division $0/2=0$, square 0, exponent 0. The weight is $e^0=1$. We moved the whole bell so that the selected point became its peak.

**Width $\sigma=1$.** Displacement $4-2=2$, relative displacement $2/1=2$, square 4, exponent −2. The weight is $e^{-2}\approx0.135335$. The bell became narrower, and this point's weight decreased.

**Width $\sigma=4$.** Displacement 2, relative displacement $2/4=0.5$, square $0.5\cdot0.5=0.25$, exponent $-0.25/2=-0.125$. The weight is $e^{-0.125}\approx0.882497$. The point is only half a width from the center, so its weight increased.

**Width $\sigma=0$.** The operation $2/0$ is already undefined. The check stops the function before division. This is not weight 0, infinite weight, or a valid Gaussian.

</details>

### How to Read Very Small Numbers

The lab may show a small number as `1.523e-8`. Here, the letter `e` is **part of Python's number notation**, not a separate factor $e\approx2.71828$.

This reads as “1.523 times ten to the power of minus eight”:

$$
1.523\mathrm{e}{-8}
=1.523\cdot10^{-8}
=\frac{1.523}{100\,000\,000}
=0.00000001523.
$$

We already know how to read negative powers: $10^{-8}$ is one divided by eight tens multiplied together. This format shows a small positive result without a long string of zeros.

In the tables above, `.6f` rounds printed output to six decimal places. A very small number can therefore appear as `0.000000` while remaining positive internally. The last function's output uses `.6g`: six significant digits, switching to the short notation when needed. Rounding the display is different from an actual value rounding down to zero inside a calculation.

## 14. A Few Changes to the Formula

Each of the following changes can be traced through the same five operations: subtract, divide, square, divide by 2 and negate, then calculate the exponential.

### Exercise 1. The Same Coordinates in Different Units

In the first case, $x=4$ cm, $\mu=2$ cm, $\sigma=2$ cm. In the second, the same quantities are written in meters: $x=0.04$, $\mu=0.02$, $\sigma=0.02$. Does the weight change?

<details>
<summary>Worked answer</summary>

In centimeters, displacement is $4-2=2$, and relative displacement is $2/2=1$. Then the square is 1, the exponent is −0.5, and the weight is approximately 0.606531.

In meters, displacement is $0.04-0.02=0.02$, and relative displacement is $0.02/0.02=1$. Every following operation is identical: square 1, exponent −0.5, weight approximately 0.606531.

The physical position relative to the width did not change. Only the way we wrote the lengths changed. The conversion applies to **all three** quantities; centimeters and meters cannot be mixed in one ratio.

</details>

### Exercise 2. What Breaks Without the Square?

With center 2 and width 2, we omit the square for points 4 and 0: the relative displacement goes straight through division by 2, negation, and the exponential. Will symmetry and a peak of 1 survive?

<details>
<summary>Worked answer</summary>

For point 4: displacement $4-2=2$, relative displacement $2/2=1$. Without squaring, the exponent is $-1/2=-0.5$, and the result is approximately 0.606531.

For point 0: displacement $0-2=-2$, relative displacement $-2/2=-1$. Without squaring, the exponent is $-(-1)/2=+0.5$, and the result is $e^{0.5}=\sqrt{e}\approx1.648721$.

Equal distances give different values. On the left, the weight even exceeds 1 and becomes greater than the center's value. We've lost our symmetric bell. That's why we needed the square.

</details>

### Exercise 3. What Breaks Without the Minus Sign?

This time the square stays, but the minus sign before division disappears. What happens at the center and one width away?

<details>
<summary>Worked answer</summary>

At the center, relative displacement is 0, its square is 0, and the exponent is $0/2=0$. The result is 1.

One width away, relative displacement is 1 or −1; either square is 1. Without the minus sign, the exponent is $1/2=+0.5$, giving approximately 1.648721. Two widths away, the square is 4, the exponent is $4/2=2$, and the result is $e^2\approx7.389056$.

Influence grows with distance. Symmetry remains, but the center becomes a minimum. The minus sign converted the increasing squared separation into a decreasing weight.

</details>

### Exercise 4. If Width Doubles, Does the Peak Become Half as High?

And can we say that the Gaussian ends beyond three widths?

<details>
<summary>Worked answer</summary>

No. At the center, $x=\mu$, so displacement is 0. For any positive width, $0/\sigma=0$, the square is 0, the exponent is 0, and the result is $e^0=1$. Increasing width stretches the profile without changing our fixed peak height.

At three widths, relative displacement is 3, its square is 9, the exponent is −4.5, and the weight is approximately 0.011109. It is small but positive. Farther away, the weight keeps decreasing smoothly rather than stopping. Truncating the tail is a separate approximation in a particular program, not a property of the formula.

</details>

title: Lesson 3. A Gaussian on a Plane: From a Bell Curve to a Spot

cells.source:
In the previous lesson, we moved along a ruler and calculated a weight at each point. An image needs more than one ruler: we can move right, or we can move up. We'll add a second coordinate and see how the familiar bell curve becomes a soft spot.

We'll start with a map, a hill, and slices of the same function. Then we'll pick one point and calculate its weight in two ways. The operations are familiar: subtract, divide, square, and take an exponential. The new part is how we combine the two directions.

## 1. One Spot: Color, Height, and Slices

The map shows weight as color: dark areas are weak, bright areas are strong. Contours on the map join points of equal weight. The “Second view” menu switches between a hill and two slices. The hill draws the same weight as height. **The hill's height is the function's value, not a third coordinate of an object.** We're still working on a plane.

The orange point marks the calculation location. A white plus marks the spot's center. The calculation for the selected point appears beneath the plots; we'll work through each row shortly.

display(plane_figure(language=LANG))
display(plane_lab(language=LANG))

Four parameter changes reveal different parts of the picture:

1. In the **“Circle”** example, the two scales are equal, so the spot spreads out equally in all directions.
2. In the starting example, the scale along $x$ is 2, and along $y$ it is 1. The contours stretch to the left and right. The peak stays at height 1.
3. We move the center's $y$ coordinate from 0 to 1. The spot moves up. The orange point stays where it was, so the weight at that point changes.
4. After a reset, we change only “Point: x” and “Point: y.” The spot now stays in place; only the location where we sample it changes.

Coordinates range from −5 to 5 in every view. A slice has a coordinate on its horizontal axis and weight on its vertical axis. The weight scale stays between 0 and 1, and the color scale stays fixed too. An expanding spot therefore cannot hide behind an automatic change in the plot's scale.

The calculations below use the starting example: center $(0,0)$, scales 2 and 1, point $(2,1)$.

## 2. Two Coordinates Instead of One

The pair $(2,1)$ has an order: first $x=2$, then $y=1$. From the origin, we move two units right and one unit up. Positive $y$ points upward in this lesson. Image arrays often count rows downward from the top; we'll return to that different convention when we work with pixels.

The center now has two numbers too: $(\mu_x,\mu_y)$. The small letters below are called **subscripts**. Here they only name the direction: $\mu_x$ is “mu along x,” and $\mu_y$ is “mu along y.” They do not mean multiplication by $x$ or $y$.

| Notation | How to read it | Our values |
|---|---|---|
| $(x,y)$ | Point coordinates | $(2,1)$ |
| $(\mu_x,\mu_y)$ | Center coordinates | $(0,0)$ |
| $\sigma_x$ | “sigma x,” the horizontal width scale | 2 |
| $\sigma_y$ | “sigma y,” the vertical width scale | 1 |
| $f(x,y)$ | “f of x and y,” the weight at this point | Not calculated yet |

The function takes two numbers and returns **one**. Both the map's color and the hill's height show that one number.

We'll measure the point, center, and scales in the same units, such as centimeters. The demo uses arbitrary units. Both scales must be greater than zero. For now, the width directions line up with the $x$ and $y$ axes; we'll rotate the spot in the next lesson.

## 3. One Bell Curve for Each Direction

For now, we set the vertical direction aside. Horizontally, everything works just as in lesson 2:

$$
d_x=x-\mu_x=2-0=2,
\qquad u_x=\frac{d_x}{\sigma_x}=\frac{2}{2}=1.
$$

$d_x$ is the horizontal offset. $u_x$ is the same offset measured in scale units. Two centimeters with a two-centimeter scale means one scale unit. Next come the square, division by 2, minus sign, and exponential:

$$
w_x=\exp\left(-\frac{u_x^2}{2}\right)
=\exp\left(-\frac{1\cdot1}{2}\right)
=\exp(-0.5)\approx0.606531.
$$

$w_x$ is a short name for the weight based **only on the horizontal direction**. Now we repeat the calculation vertically:

$$
d_y=y-\mu_y=1-0=1,
\qquad u_y=\frac{d_y}{\sigma_y}=\frac{1}{1}=1.
$$

$$
w_y=\exp\left(-\frac{u_y^2}{2}\right)
=\exp\left(-\frac{1\cdot1}{2}\right)
=\exp(-0.5)\approx0.606531.
$$

We moved two coordinate units horizontally and one vertically, but the offsets **in scale units** are the same. That's why the two weights match.

For our spot, we multiply them:

$$
f(x,y)=w_x\cdot w_y.
$$

Moving away along either direction now reduces the combined weight. If we're exactly at the center along one axis, its weight is 1, so multiplication leaves the other axis's weight unchanged. If we move away along both axes, the two reductions act together.

At $(2,1)$, this gives approximately $0.606531\cdot0.606531\approx0.367879$. We won't multiply already rounded numbers in the calculation. Python will retain its full precision, and we'll use six decimal places only when printing.

ux = (2 - 0) / 2
uy = (1 - 0) / 1
weight_x = math.exp(-(ux * ux) / 2)
weight_y = math.exp(-(uy * uy) / 2)
print(f"wx = {weight_x:.6f}")
print(f"wy = {weight_y:.6f}")
print(f"wx * wy = {weight_x * weight_y:.6f}")

## 4. Why a Sum Appears Inside the Formula

We multiplied two weights, yet the compact formula will contain an addition. The calculation hasn't changed. When powers with the same base are multiplied, **their exponents add**.

For whole-number exponents, we can count the factors:

$$
2^2\cdot2^3=(2\cdot2)\cdot(2\cdot2\cdot2)=2^5=2^{2+3}.
$$

Fractional and negative powers follow the same rule. For example, $e^{-0.5}=1/\sqrt{e}$, so:

$$
e^{-0.5}\cdot e^{-0.5}
=\frac{1}{\sqrt{e}}\cdot\frac{1}{\sqrt{e}}
=\frac{1}{e}=e^{-1}.
$$

The two exponents, each $-0.5$, add to $-1$. In general, the rule is $e^a\cdot e^b=e^{a+b}$. Here, $a$ and $b$ stand for any two exponents.

We substitute our expressions for them. We can follow the whole change one line at a time:

$$
\begin{aligned}
f(x,y)&=\exp\left(-\frac{u_x^2}{2}\right)\cdot\exp\left(-\frac{u_y^2}{2}\right)\\
&=\exp\left(-\frac{u_x^2}{2}-\frac{u_y^2}{2}\right)\\
&=\exp\left(-\frac{u_x^2+u_y^2}{2}\right).
\end{aligned}
$$

In the last line, both fractions have the same denominator, 2. We add their numerators and keep the common division. We are adding **squared offsets inside the exponent**, not adding the finished weights outside it.

## 5. Building the Formula from the Inside

Now we replace $u_x$ and $u_y$ with the operations they stand for:

$$
f(x,y)=\exp\left[-\frac12\left(
\left(\frac{x-\mu_x}{\sigma_x}\right)^2+
\left(\frac{y-\mu_y}{\sigma_y}\right)^2
\right)\right].
$$

The square brackets work just like round parentheses here: they group the expression passed to the exponential. The two fractions describe the two directions. Each small superscript 2 applies to **the whole fraction**, including its denominator.

The calculation follows this order:

1. We subtract the center separately from $x$ and $y$.
2. We divide each offset by the scale for **its own** direction.
3. We square both resulting numbers.
4. We add the two squares.
5. We divide the sum by 2, put a minus sign in front, and evaluate the exponential.

Calling the sum of squares $q$ gives us a name for the intermediate value:

$$
q=u_x^2+u_y^2,
\qquad f(x,y)=\exp(-q/2).
$$

$u_x$ and $u_y$ are dimensionless: centimeters canceled when divided by centimeters. Their squares, the sum $q$, the exponent $-q/2$, and the final weight have no units of length either.

At the center, both offsets are zero. Then $q=0^2+0^2=0$ and $f(\mu_x,\mu_y)=e^0=1$. Moving in any direction makes at least one square positive. The exponent becomes negative, and the weight becomes less than 1. Changing the scales still preserves the peak of 1.

## 6. Working Through the Point $(2,1)$ Without Skipping Steps

The center is $(0,0)$, with scales $\sigma_x=2$ and $\sigma_y=1$. Both coordinates and scales use the same units.

| Step | Horizontal direction | Vertical direction |
|---|---|---|
| Subtracting the center | $d_x=2-0=2$ | $d_y=1-0=1$ |
| Dividing by the corresponding scale | $u_x=2/2=1$ | $u_y=1/1=1$ |
| Squaring | $u_x^2=1\cdot1=1$ | $u_y^2=1\cdot1=1$ |

Now the two branches join:

$$
q=1+1=2,\qquad -q/2=-2/2=-1,
\qquad f(2,1)=e^{-1}\approx0.367879.
$$

On the heatmap, this number determines the color at the orange point. On the hill, it is the marked point's height. On the same map, the point lies between the lines for weights of approximately 0.607 and 0.135.

Each operation gets a separate Python line. `qx` and `qy` hold the squares, `exponent` holds the exponent, and `weight` holds the final weight. Here, `*` means multiplication, `/` means division, and `=` stores the expression on the right in the variable on the left.

x, y = 2.0, 1.0
mux, muy = 0.0, 0.0
sx, sy = 2.0, 1.0

dx = x - mux
dy = y - muy
ux = dx / sx
uy = dy / sy
qx = ux * ux
qy = uy * uy
q = qx + qy
exponent = -q / 2
weight = math.exp(exponent)

print(f"dx = {dx:.1f}, dy = {dy:.1f}")
print(f"ux = {ux:.1f}, uy = {uy:.1f}")
print(f"qx = {qx:.1f}, qy = {qy:.1f}")
print(f"q = {q:.1f}, exponent = {exponent:.1f}")
print(f"weight = {weight:.6f}")

## 7. From a Circle to an Ellipse

Equal-weight contours are drawn on the heatmap. We take the one where the weight equals $e^{-1/2}\approx0.606531$. We already know that this weight occurs when $q=1$. The points on our chosen curve therefore satisfy:

$$
\left(\frac{x-\mu_x}{\sigma_x}\right)^2+
\left(\frac{y-\mu_y}{\sigma_y}\right)^2=1.
$$

A **contour** is a line of equal values. Crossing it does not turn off the Gaussian: the weight keeps decreasing beyond it.

When both scales equal 1 and the center is at the origin, the condition becomes $x^2+y^2=1$. This is a circle of radius 1. The connection to distance comes from the Pythagorean theorem: the square of a right triangle's diagonal side equals the sum of the squares of its other two sides. For example, moving 3 units right and 4 units up gives $3^2+4^2=9+16=25$, so the distance from the origin is $\sqrt{25}=5$. A constant sum $x^2+y^2$ therefore means a constant distance from the origin.

Now we stretch the horizontal direction by a factor of two: $\sigma_x=2$, $\sigma_y=1$. After division, the point $(2,0)$ becomes $(1,0)$, while $(0,1)$ remains $(0,1)$. Both have a sum of squared scaled coordinates equal to 1. In the original coordinates, the circle has become an **ellipse**.

For this contour, the distance from the center to the rightmost point is $\sigma_x$, and to the topmost point it is $\sigma_y$. These segments are called **semiaxes**. The contour's full horizontal width is $2\sigma_x$, and its full vertical height is $2\sigma_y$. These are the dimensions of one particular level curve; the entire soft spot still has no finite boundary.
display(ellipse_figure(language=LANG))

We can check a point between the axis endpoints too. For the ellipse, the figure's table uses $(\sqrt{2},1/\sqrt{2})$, approximately $(1.414214,0.707107)$.

For this point:

$$
u_x=\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}},
\qquad u_y=\frac{1/\sqrt{2}}{1}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}.
$$

We can check the first equality by multiplying both sides by $\sqrt{2}$: the left becomes $\sqrt{2}\cdot\sqrt{2}/2=2/2=1$, and the right becomes 1 too. Squaring each number gives $1/2$:

$$
q=\left(\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\right)^2+
\left(\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\right)^2
=\frac12+\frac12=1.
$$

The weight is again $e^{-1/2}\approx0.606531$, so the point lies on the same contour.

By contrast, $(2,1)$ gives $1^2+1^2=2$, for a weight of about 0.367879. Moving one scale unit along **both** axes takes us farther from the center than moving one scale unit along just one axis. The corner of a rectangle with half-width 2 and half-height 1 lies outside the ellipse.

The value 0.606531 means roughly 61% **of the peak weight**. It does not mean that the ellipse contains 61% of an area or a probability.

## 8. A Slice Through the Spot Reveals the Familiar Bell Curve

The “Two slices” option under “Second view” shows horizontal and vertical sections through the selected point. The dashed reference curves pass through the spot’s center.

We can draw a horizontal line on the heatmap and move only along it. Then $y$ stays fixed while $x$ changes. This is a **slice** of the function: we're examining the plane along one chosen line.

If the line passes through the center, $y=\mu_y$, then the vertical offset is zero, $u_y=0$, and $w_y=e^0=1$. That gives:

$$
f(x,\mu_y)=w_x\cdot1=w_x.
$$

This is exactly the one-dimensional Gaussian from the previous lesson. Its center along $x$ is $\mu_x$, its scale is $\sigma_x$, and its peak is 1.

But a slice does not have to pass through the peak. We fix $y=1$, with $\mu_y=0$ and $\sigma_y=1$. Then $u_y=(1-0)/1=1$, so $w_y=e^{-1/2}\approx0.606531$ at **every** point on this horizontal line. It simply multiplies the whole horizontal bell curve:

$$
f(x,1)=w_x\cdot0.606531\ldots
$$

Its peak is now about 0.606531, even though the complete two-dimensional function still peaks at 1. That peak remains at $(0,0)$, outside the chosen line. The slice's width along $x$ has not changed.

The vertical slice works the same way. With $x=2$ fixed, the horizontal weight $w_x\approx0.606531$ multiplies the vertical bell curve. Both slices cross at $(2,1)$, so they must give the same weight there: approximately 0.367879.
display(slices_figure(mux=0, muy=0, sx=2, sy=1, x=2, y=1, language=LANG))

## 9. How One Number Changes the Weight

We return to point $(2,1)$, center $(0,0)$, and scales 2 and 1. Before any changes, the weight is approximately 0.367879.

**We narrow only the horizontal scale to $\sigma_x=1$.** The offsets are still $d_x=2$ and $d_y=1$. But now $u_x=2/1=2$, while $u_y=1/1=1$. Then $q=2^2+1^2=4+1=5$, the exponent is $-5/2=-2.5$, and the weight is $e^{-2.5}\approx0.082085$. The point is farther away in units of the new horizontal scale.

**We restore $\sigma_x=2$ and widen the vertical scale to $\sigma_y=2$.** We get $u_x=2/2=1$ and $u_y=1/2=0.5$. The squares, 1 and 0.25, give $q=1.25$, the exponent is $-1.25/2=-0.625$, and the weight is $e^{-0.625}\approx0.535261$. Vertically, the same point is now closer in scale units, so the combined weight increases.

**We restore scales 2 and 1, then move the center to $(1,-1)$.** At the original point $(2,1)$, the offsets become $d_x=2-1=1$ and $d_y=1-(-1)=2$. Thus $u_x=1/2=0.5$, $u_y=2/1=2$, the sum is $q=0.25+4=4.25$, the exponent is $-2.125$, and the weight is approximately 0.119433.

If we move the point by the same offset $(1,-1)$ as the center, it ends up at $(3,0)$. The differences return to $3-1=2$ and $0-(-1)=1$, so the weight returns to 0.367879. What matters is the offset **from the center**, not where the whole arrangement sits relative to the origin.

## 10. A Function for Any Point

We can put the calculation into a function. It takes two point coordinates, two center coordinates, and two scales. All six numbers must be finite, and both scales must be positive.

The `math.isfinite` check rejects infinity and `NaN`, a special value meaning “not a number.” `all` checks that the condition holds for each of the six values. The remaining lines repeat the operations we've already worked out by hand.

The demo gives the same numbers. The final point, $(-2,-1)$, is the reflection of $(2,1)$ through the center. The offsets change sign, but their squares match, so the weights match too.

A zero scale produces a `ValueError`: we cannot divide by zero. The call `plane_weight(2, 1, 0, 0, 0, 1)` demonstrates the check: it returns an error message instead of a weight. With a positive scale, the calculation works again.

The screen shows only the square from −5 to 5. The Gaussian itself does not end at that square's edge. Beyond three scale units, for example, the weight is small but mathematically still positive. A computer may round extremely small results down to zero, as we saw in the previous lesson.

For now, we're defining a spatial weight with a peak of 1. Color, opacity, and overlapping spots arrive in lesson 5. No training takes place here: we're changing every parameter ourselves.

## 11. A Few Checks Before Looking at the Slider

The questions use center $(0,0)$ and scales $\sigma_x=2$, $\sigma_y=1$ unless stated otherwise. Each experiment starts with a prediction, followed by a calculation and a comparison with the figure.

### 1. Two Different Points, One Weight

Do points $(2,0)$ and $(0,1)$ have the same weight, or is one greater?

<details>
<summary>Worked answer</summary>

At the first point, $u_x=2/2=1$ and $u_y=0/1=0$, so $q=1^2+0^2=1$. At the second, $u_x=0/2=0$ and $u_y=1/1=1$, so $q=0^2+1^2=1$. Both give exponent $-1/2=-0.5$ and weight $e^{-0.5}\approx0.606531$. The coordinate distances differ, but each direction's scale accounts for that.

</details>

### 2. At the Corner

Both previous points lie on the 0.606531 contour. Will $(2,1)$ lie on it too?

<details>
<summary>Worked answer</summary>

At $(2,1)$, $u_x=1$ and $u_y=1$, so $q=1+1=2$. The exponent is $-2/2=-1$, and the weight is $e^{-1}\approx0.367879$. This point lies outside the chosen contour. Both departures from the center count together.

</details>

### 3. Moving Everything Together

The center moves to $(1,-1)$ and the point to $(3,0)$. The scales stay the same. Does the weight differ from the original point $(2,1)$ with center $(0,0)$?

<details>
<summary>Worked answer</summary>

The new offsets are $3-1=2$ and $0-(-1)=1$, matching the original ones. Dividing by the scales again gives 1 and 1, the sum of squares is 2, the exponent is −1, and the weight is approximately 0.367879. Moving both together preserves the point's position relative to the spot.

</details>

### 4. A Slice Misses the Peak

With $y=2$ fixed, what is the horizontal slice's maximum height? What weight does it show at $x=2$?

<details>
<summary>Worked answer</summary>

The vertical offset is $d_y=2-0=2$, its scaled value is $u_y=2/1=2$, its square is 4, and the vertical weight is $w_y=e^{-4/2}=e^{-2}\approx0.135335$.

The horizontal weight reaches its maximum of 1 at $x=\mu_x=0$. The slice therefore peaks at $1\cdot0.135335\approx0.135335$. At $x=2$, the horizontal offset in scale units is 1, giving total $q=1^2+2^2=5$, exponent −2.5, and weight approximately 0.082085. A low slice does not mean that the hill's overall peak has disappeared.

</details>

### 5. What If We Add the Finished Weights?

Replacing the product with $(w_x+w_y)/2$ gives 1 at the center, which looks promising. What happens at point $(0,3)$?

<details>
<summary>Worked answer</summary>

Horizontally, $u_x=0$, so $w_x=1$. Vertically, $u_y=3/1=3$, the square is 9, the exponent is $-9/2=-4.5$, and $w_y\approx0.011109$.

The mean gives $(1+0.011109)/2\approx0.505555$: about half the peak, even far away vertically. The product gives $1\cdot0.011109=0.011109$. Averaging leaves long, prominent strips along the axes because a large weight in one direction offsets a small one in the other. We chose multiplication for a spot that fades as we move away along either direction.

</details>

## 12. What We Added to the One-Dimensional Bell

We repeated the familiar calculation for two directions and combined the results. We can now pick a point on the color map, locate it on the hill, and explain its weight using two offsets and two scales. The visible ellipse comes from the same numbers that appear in the formula.

So far, the ellipse is tied to the horizontal and vertical axes. In [lesson 4](#/en/4), we'll rotate it. A covariance matrix will appear, but we'll start with a picture and a few points again: what numbers do we need to describe our familiar shape after it turns?

title: Lesson 4 — Rotating a Spot and Unpacking Its Covariance Matrix

cells.source:
In the previous lesson, we stretched a circle into an ellipse. Its long side always stayed along one of the coordinate axes, though. What if we want to draw a sloping branch or the edge of a roof?

We'll rotate the spot. In the viewer, one slider does the job. Below the plot, four numbers appear inside square brackets: the **covariance matrix**. We'll connect those numbers to size and tilt, then use them to calculate the weight at a point.

First we'll look at the rotation, then perform it with ordinary multiplication and addition. The matrix will become a short way to write operations we already understand.

Along the way, we'll meet sine, cosine, and matrix multiplication. The calculation will take two forms: rotating the point back, and using the covariance matrix. One example will show why they give the same weight.

## 1. The Ellipse Rotates
display(covariance_figure(language=LANG))
display(covariance_lab(language=LANG))

The main example has **scales 2 and 1, angle 45°, point (1, 1)**. The center stays at `(0, 0)` throughout this lesson so that translation doesn't distract us from shape.

1. As the angle moves from 0° to 45°, then to −45°, the spot keeps its length and thickness. Nonzero entries appear away from the matrix diagonal, and their signs change with the direction of tilt.
2. At 45°, increasing only the first scale stretches the spot along its tilted axis, rather than straight to the right.
3. In the “Circle” example, changing the angle leaves the shape unchanged. A circle has no preferred long direction.
4. In the main example, the point `(1, 1)` stays fixed. Depending on the tilt, it lies along the long side or closer to the short side. Its weight changes accordingly.
5. In “Point at the center,” the weight is 1 for every positive pair of scales and every angle.

The orange and green arrows show the **spot's own axes**. We'll call the scales along them $s_1$ and $s_2$, read “s one” and “s two.” The subscripts simply distinguish the two axes. Initially, $s_1=2$ and $s_2=1$.

After rotation, these axes no longer match world $x$ and $y$. So we won't call $s_1$ the “width along x”: it is the scale along the first, tilted axis.

The contour joins points with weight $e^{-1/2}\approx0.607$. As in lesson 3, the spot continues beyond it. Here the line helps us compare shapes.

## 2. Why the Matrix Stores Squared Sizes

For the axis-aligned ellipse in lesson 3, we calculated the following from offsets $d_x$ and $d_y$:

$$
q=\left(\frac{d_x}{s_1}\right)^2+\left(\frac{d_y}{s_2}\right)^2,
\qquad f=\exp(-q/2).
$$

$d_x=x-\mu_x$ and $d_y=y-\mu_y$ tell us how far the point is displaced from the center in each direction. $\mu_x,\mu_y$ are the center coordinates. For now, both are zero, so $d_x=x$ and $d_y=y$.

Squaring the fractions puts $s_1^2$ and $s_2^2$ in their denominators. With scales 2 and 1, these are $2\cdot2=4$ and $1\cdot1=1$. Those squares will form the diagonal of the unrotated spot's matrix.

The word **variance** comes from measuring spread. For a small collection of numbers, −2, −2, 2, 2, the mean is:

$$
\bar x=\frac{-2-2+2+2}{4}=0.
$$

The bar over $x$ means “mean x.” We subtract the mean from each number, square each difference, and average the results:

$$
v_x=\frac{(-2-0)^2+(-2-0)^2+(2-0)^2+(2-0)^2}{4}
=\frac{4+4+4+4}{4}=4.
$$

This is the **variance**: the mean squared deviation from the mean. It measures spread, but in squared units. If the coordinates are centimeters, the variance is 4 cm². Taking the square root returns us to centimeters: $\sqrt4=2$ cm. This is the **standard deviation**.

For a Gaussian, the scale $s$ is defined so that $s^2$ is the variance of the normalized distribution with that shape. We're still drawing an unnormalized weight with a peak of 1; we don't need the probability-density prefactor here.

The four numbers above let us see the arithmetic of spread. They do not become a Gaussian, nor are they required points of one. We choose our spot's scales ourselves.

## 3. Covariance: Do the Two Coordinates Change Together?

Now we have four points on a plane:

| Point | x | y | x² | x·y | y² |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| A | −2 | −1 | 4 | 2 | 1 |
| B | −2 | 1 | 4 | −2 | 1 |
| C | 2 | −1 | 4 | −2 | 1 |
| D | 2 | 1 | 4 | 2 | 1 |
| Mean | 0 | 0 | 4 | 0 | 1 |

Both mean coordinates are zero, so deviations from the mean equal $x$ and $y$ themselves.

The $x^2$ and $y^2$ columns give variances 4 and 1. The $x\cdot y$ column asks a different question: **do the two coordinate deviations have matching signs?** Two positive or two negative deviations give a positive product. Opposite signs give a negative product.

The average of those products is the **covariance**:

$$
b=\frac{2-2-2+2}{4}=0.
$$

The positive and negative contributions cancel. This set favors neither an “up and right” nor a “down and right” tilt.

If the set is not centered at zero, we first subtract its means. In general:

$$
b=\frac1N\sum_{i=1}^{N}(x_i-\bar x)(y_i-\bar y).
$$

Here $N$ is the number of points; $i$ is the current point's index; $x_i,y_i$ are its coordinates; and $\sum$ (“sigma”) denotes the sum of the results for every index from 1 to N. For each point, we subtract the means and multiply the two deviations. We then add all the products and divide by the number of points.

We are describing **the entire given set**, so we divide by $N=4$. When estimating an unknown covariance from a random sample, statistics often uses $N-1$. That is a different task; we must not switch divisors halfway through this example.

Covariance also has units of cm² if both coordinates use centimeters. It is not an angle in degrees. Its relation to tilt also involves the two variances: the single number $b$ does not determine the whole ellipse.

## 4. Four Numbers Instead of Three Long Labels

The numbers fit into a table with two rows and two columns:

$$
\Sigma=
\begin{bmatrix}
v_x & b\\
b & v_y
\end{bmatrix}
=\begin{bmatrix}4&0\\0&1\end{bmatrix}.
$$

Capital $\Sigma$ is read “sigma.” Here it names the entire matrix, unlike the small $\sigma$ from lesson 2. A matrix is a rectangular array of numbers; below, we'll define how to perform operations with it.

- The upper-left entry is variance along world $x$.
- The lower-right entry is variance along world $y$.
- The remaining entries are covariance. They match because $x\cdot y$ and $y\cdot x$ give the same product.

The line from the upper-left entry to the lower-right one is the **main diagonal**. A matrix whose entries match across this diagonal is **symmetric**.

For our unrotated spot:

$$
D=\begin{bmatrix}s_1^2&0\\0&s_2^2\end{bmatrix}
=\begin{bmatrix}4&0\\0&1\end{bmatrix}.
$$

We'll reserve $D$ for the matrix in the spot's own axes. In $\mathrm{diag}(4,1)$, `diag` denotes a matrix with 4 and 1 on the diagonal and zeros in the remaining entries.

While the spot's axes match $x,y$, $D$ and $\Sigma$ are identical. After rotation, $D$ keeps its 4 and 1, while $\Sigma$, the shape written in world coordinates, changes.

## 5. Rotation Before Matrices: Two Projections of an Arrow

An arrow of length 1 initially points right, with its tip at `(1, 0)`. We rotate it counterclockwise through an angle $\theta$, pronounced “theta.”

A full turn is 360°, and a quarter turn is 90°. At 45°, the arrow points halfway between right and up.

After rotation, its tip has coordinates:

$$
(\cos\theta,\ \sin\theta).
$$

**Cosine** is the horizontal coordinate of the unit arrow's tip; **sine** is its vertical coordinate. These are signed projections: the horizontal coordinate is negative on the left, and the vertical coordinate is negative below zero.

| Angle | cos θ | sin θ | Direction of the first axis |
|---|---:|---:|---|
| 0° | 1 | 0 | Right |
| 90° | 0 | 1 | Up |
| 180° | −1 | 0 | Left |
| −90° | 0 | −1 | Down |

At 45°, the two projections match. For a right triangle, the square of the sloping side's length equals the sum of the squares of the other two sides. Our arrow has length 1, so $c^2+c^2=1$: first $2c^2=1$, then $c^2=1/2$, then $c=1/\sqrt2\approx0.707107$. We take the positive root because the arrow points up and right. Thus $\cos45°=\sin45°=1/\sqrt2$.

Below we'll shorten the notation to $c=\cos\theta$ and $s=\sin\theta$. Here $s$ **without a subscript** means sine; the spot's scales are still $s_1,s_2$.
display(rotation_figure(angle_deg=45, language=LANG))

The second axis must be perpendicular to the first. If the first points along $(c,s)$, the second points along $(-s,c)$. At 45° this is `(-0.707107, 0.707107)`, up and left. Both arrows have length 1.

A point lies $a$ units along the first axis and $b$ units along the second. Here $a,b$ are the point's coordinates in the spot's frame; we'll set aside the covariance symbol $b$ for a moment. We add the two displacements:

$$
\begin{aligned}
x&=ca-sb,\\
y&=sa+cb.
\end{aligned}
$$

For example, $(a,b)=(2,0)$ at 45° gives $x=0.707107\cdot2-0.707107\cdot0\approx1.414214$ and $y=0.707107\cdot2+0.707107\cdot0\approx1.414214$.

The numbers 2 and 0 have not changed as coordinates along the spot's own axes. We've worked out where that same point lies in world coordinates.

## 6. The Same Rotation Written as a Matrix

The coefficients of our two operations form a table:

$$
R=\begin{bmatrix}c&-s\\s&c\end{bmatrix},
\qquad
\begin{bmatrix}x\\y\end{bmatrix}
=R\begin{bmatrix}a\\b\end{bmatrix}.
$$

$R$ names the rotation matrix. Two numbers written vertically form a **column vector**. Here it simply stores two coordinates.

Matrix–vector multiplication works **row against column**. For the first output coordinate, we multiply each entry of the first row by the matching entry of the column and add: $c\cdot a+(-s)\cdot b$. For the second, we use the second row: $s\cdot a+c\cdot b$. This performs exactly the geometric operation from the previous section.

The columns of $R$ have a meaning too: the first tells us where the unit arrow `(1,0)` went, and the second tells us where `(0,1)` went.

Python's `@` operator performs this matrix multiplication. Ordinary `*` between NumPy arrays multiplies matching entries, so it cannot replace `@` here.

`math.sin` and `math.cos` take angles **in radians**. One radian is an angle whose arc on a circle of radius 1 has length 1. A full circle has arc length $2\pi$, so 360° is $2\pi$ radians. Thus 180° is $\pi$, and 45° is $\pi/4\approx0.785398$. The number $\pi\approx3.141593$ is a circle's circumference divided by its diameter. `math.radians` handles the conversion for us.

theta_deg = 45.0
theta_rad = math.radians(theta_deg)
c = math.cos(theta_rad)
s = math.sin(theta_rad)
R = np.array([[c, -s], [s, c]])
local_point = np.array([2.0, 0.0])
world_point = R @ local_point
print("angle in radians =", round(theta_rad, 6))
print("cos, sin =", round(c, 6), round(s, 6))
print("R =\n", np.round(R, 6))
print("world point =", np.round(world_point, 6))

## 7. Calculating Weight by Rotating the Point Back

We can now turn coordinates along the spot's axes into world coordinates. But the viewer gives us a world point. To use the formula from lesson 3, we need its offsets **along the ellipse's own axes**.

We first subtract the center, then rotate that offset through **the negative of the same angle**. For a rotation matrix, its transpose does this:

$$
R^T=\begin{bmatrix}c&s\\-s&c\end{bmatrix}.
$$

The superscript $T$ means “transpose,” not a power. Rows become columns: the upper-right and lower-left entries exchange places. For a rotation matrix, this gives the reverse rotation; for an arbitrary matrix, transposing does not replace taking the inverse.

We write the world offset as a column $d$ and call its coordinates after the reverse rotation $d_1,d_2$:

$$
d=\begin{bmatrix}d_x\\d_y\end{bmatrix},
\qquad
\begin{bmatrix}d_1\\d_2\end{bmatrix}
=R^Td
=\begin{bmatrix}cd_x+sd_y\\-sd_x+cd_y\end{bmatrix}.
$$

For `(1,1)`, center `(0,0)`, and angle 45°, the calculation goes as follows. We'll use the exact values $c=s=1/\sqrt2$ and round only for display:

$$
\begin{aligned}
d_x&=1-0=1,\qquad d_y=1-0=1,\\
